title: Xinzuo Academy
subtitle: Interactive staff training from The Gongfu of Xinzuo

levels.title: Base
levels.purpose: Safe, accurate product knowledge and correct everyday knife use.

modules.title: Safety & Control
modules.summary: Build predictable habits before speed: stable workstation, stable food, correct tool, controlled force and safe handling.

content.lead: Many knife accidents begin before the blade touches food.
points: Stabilize the board before cutting.
Keep the cutting path clear and the work area dry and well lit.
Dry hands and handle, stabilize the food, choose the correct knife, then identify the blade path.
content.takeaway: Stable board. Stable food. Clear path. Hidden fingertips.

question.prompt: What should happen before the first cut?

options.text: Start slowly and stabilize the board only if it moves.
Stabilize the board and food, clear the blade path, then choose and position the knife.
Hold the food firmly and use extra downward pressure.
Wet the board so the knife cannot bounce.

question.explanation: Safety starts before cutting. The board, ingredient and cutting path must already be controlled.

recovery_questions.prompt: The board moves slightly when you begin slicing. What is the correct response?

options.text: Grip the knife more tightly.
Stop and stabilize the board before continuing.
Use shorter, faster strokes.
Move the food closer to the board edge.

recovery_questions.explanation: A moving board makes every later movement less predictable. Correct the workstation first.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which check best matches the Academy safety rule?

options.text: Sharp knife, fast cut, strong grip, clean board.
Stable board, stable food, clear path, hidden fingertips.
Heavy knife, dry food, straight edge, wide stance.
Large board, soft steel, slow cut, open fingertips.

recovery_questions.explanation: The four-part rule is a compact pre-cut check, not a performance technique.

content.lead: Round and irregular ingredients can move under the blade.
points: Create a flat surface on round produce before the main cuts.
Divide large or irregular food into manageable sections.
Do not force a fine kitchen knife into unsuitable frozen food.
content.takeaway: If the ingredient can roll, the cut is not ready to begin.

question.prompt: What is the safest first action with a round potato that rolls on the board?

options.text: Hold it harder with the fingertips.
Use a heavier knife.
Create a flat face and place that face on the board.
Start with the tip and increase speed.

question.explanation: A flat face turns an unstable ingredient into a predictable one before the main cutting starts.

recovery_questions.prompt: A large irregular vegetable cannot be held securely. What should you do?

options.text: Use more force so the knife finishes in one stroke.
Divide it into manageable, stable sections before continuing.
Change to a flexible knife.
Support it with fingers directly in the cutting line.

recovery_questions.explanation: The geometry of the task should be made stable before adding force.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is a flat base useful on an onion, melon or potato?

options.text: It makes the steel harder.
It reduces food adhesion.
It reduces rolling and makes the cutting path more predictable.
It allows sideways scraping.

recovery_questions.explanation: The goal is mechanical stability, not cutting speed.

lessons.title: Use the right knife and avoid lateral stress

content.lead: A knife can be strong in the intended cutting direction and vulnerable to twisting or levering.
points: Do not use kitchen knives as pry bars, screwdrivers, can openers or levers.
Do not twist a blade free when it binds in dense food.
Do not scrape the board sideways with the cutting edge; use the spine, blade face or a bench scraper.
content.takeaway: Choose geometry for the task and keep load aligned with the cut.

question.prompt: A thin hard blade becomes stuck in dense food. What is the correct action?

options.text: Twist the handle gently until the food opens.
Strike the spine with the free hand.
Withdraw it carefully and adjust the cut.
Push sideways with the blade face.

question.explanation: Twisting creates lateral stress. Withdraw and change the cut instead of levering the blade.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which use is inappropriate for a fine kitchen knife?

options.text: Slicing boneless meat.
Cutting vegetables on a suitable board.
Prying apart two frozen objects.
Drawing through herbs with controlled technique.

recovery_questions.explanation: A kitchen knife is a cutting tool, not a lever.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why should the cutting edge not be used to scrape food sideways across the board?

options.text: It can expose the edge to damaging lateral load.
It makes the knife too warm.
It removes the Damascus pattern.
It changes the handle balance permanently.

recovery_questions.explanation: Sideways scraping loads the fine apex in a direction it is not designed to take.

lessons.title: Set the supporting hand and use only necessary force

content.lead: Control comes from hand position and deliberate movement, not from squeezing harder.
points: Set the supporting hand before moving the knife.
Keep fingertips outside the cutting path; the claw grip is a moving guide, not a speed trick.
If a well-sharpened knife needs excessive force, stop and identify the cause.
content.takeaway: Set the hand first, then move the knife.

question.prompt: A sharp knife suddenly seems to require excessive force. What should you do?

options.text: Increase downward pressure to finish the cut.
Stop and check the edge, food stability, knife choice and movement.
Move the supporting hand closer to the edge.
Use a faster rocking motion regardless of knife profile.

question.explanation: Unexpected resistance is information. Diagnose the cause rather than compensating with force.

recovery_questions.prompt: When should the supporting hand be positioned?

options.text: After the first cut shows where the blade will travel.
Before the knife starts moving.
Only for very small ingredients.
Only when using a pinch grip.

recovery_questions.explanation: The supporting hand defines a safe path before the blade moves.

recovery_questions.prompt: What does excessive force most often tell you?

options.text: The cut should be made faster.
Something about edge condition, stability, knife choice or technique should be checked.
The handle material is wrong.
The knife needs a thicker Damascus pattern.

recovery_questions.explanation: Force is not the default solution to a cut that is behaving incorrectly.

lessons.title: Control the knife when cutting stops

content.lead: Safe habits continue during washing, passing and carrying.
points: Never leave a knife hidden under soapy water or mixed with objects in a sink.
Pass a knife deliberately with the handle oriented to the receiver and the edge clear of fingers.
For short movement, keep the knife low, close to the body, still and with the tip toward the floor.
content.takeaway: A knife must remain visible, controlled and predictable even when it is not cutting.

options.text: Washing one knife at a time while keeping the edge visible.
Carrying a knife low and still for a short distance.
Leaving a sharp knife hidden under soapy water in the sink.
Presenting the handle toward the person receiving the knife.

question.explanation: A hidden blade can injure someone who reaches into the sink without seeing it.

recovery_questions.prompt: How should a knife be carried a short distance in the kitchen?

options.text: Upright at chest height so others can see it.
Low, close to the body, still, with the tip toward the floor.
Flat on the open palm while walking.
Inside a towel held in the free hand.

recovery_questions.explanation: Low and still movement makes the knife path easier for others to predict.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is the key principle when washing a knife?

options.text: Keep the blade visible and its edge path controlled.
Soak it first so food releases by itself.
Wrap the sponge around the edge.
Place it with the other utensils before drying.

recovery_questions.explanation: Visibility and control matter more than speed during cleaning.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is the best preparation before cutting?

options.text: Choose knife → cut a test slice → stabilize food if needed.
Stabilize board → clear area → dry hands/handle → stabilize food → choose knife → identify blade path.
Stabilize food → sharpen knife → increase force → clear scraps later.
Choose the heaviest knife → wet board → hold food tightly.

questions.explanation: The complete sequence removes instability before the blade moves.

questions.prompt: A round ingredient rolls easily. What makes the task safer?

options.text: A flat supporting face.
A faster first cut.
A narrower board.
More fingertip pressure.

questions.explanation: A flat face mechanically stabilizes the ingredient.

questions.prompt: What should you do when a blade binds?

options.text: Twist gently.
Lever sideways.
Withdraw and adjust the cut.
Strike the handle.

questions.explanation: Avoid lateral stress; change the cut instead.

questions.prompt: What is the correct relationship between the supporting hand and knife movement?

options.text: Move together from the start.
Set the supporting hand first, then move the knife.
The supporting hand follows the knife.
Hand position matters only at professional speed.

questions.explanation: Hand placement establishes the safe path before movement.

questions.prompt: Which rule remains valid after cutting is finished?

options.text: Keep the knife visible and controlled during washing, passing and carrying.
A knife is safe once it is no longer moving.
The sink is the safest temporary storage place.
Carry the knife high so the blade can be seen.

questions.explanation: Non-cutting handling still requires predictable control.

modules.title: Anatomy & Bevels
modules.summary: Name the parts of a knife, distinguish construction from quality claims, and understand what bevel geometry changes.

lessons.title: Read the blade from tip to heel

content.lead: Accurate product explanation starts with accurate names.
points: The tip is the front; the spine is the upper normally unsharpened side; the blade face is the broad side.
The cutting edge is the sharpened boundary; the heel is the rear of that cutting edge.
The bevel is the geometry that narrows the blade toward the apex. Surface finish and geometry are different things.
content.takeaway: Name the feature you are discussing before describing what it does.

question.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the cutting edge from the bevel?

options.text: The bevel is the sharpened line; the cutting edge is the broad blade face.
The cutting edge is the sharpened line; the bevel is the geometry narrowing toward the apex.
They are two names for the same surface finish.
The bevel is the spine and the cutting edge is the heel.

question.explanation: The edge is the sharpened boundary; the bevel is the sloping geometry leading to it.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is the heel of a kitchen knife?

options.text: The rear of the cutting edge nearest the handle.
The rear end of the handle.
The upper unsharpened side.
The broad side of the blade.

recovery_questions.explanation: The heel is the rear portion of the cutting edge, close to the handle.

recovery_questions.prompt: Two blades have the same polished appearance. What can you safely conclude?

options.text: Their cross-section and thickness must be the same.
Their surface finish looks similar, but their geometry may still differ.
Their edge angle must be identical.
They must use the same steel.

recovery_questions.explanation: Finish is appearance/texture on the blade face; it does not prove the underlying geometry.

lessons.title: Construction is not a simple quality hierarchy

content.lead: Full tang, hidden tang, through tang and partial tang describe construction, not an automatic ranking.
points: A full tang follows almost the full handle outline and is commonly covered by scales.
A hidden tang is enclosed by the handle; a through tang reaches the butt and is not another name for full tang.
A bolster is a reinforced blade-to-handle transition on many Western knives. Its presence, absence or welding method alone does not determine knife quality.
content.takeaway: Explain how the knife is built without turning one construction feature into a universal quality score.

question.prompt: Which statement about tang construction is correct?

options.text: A through tang is simply another name for a full tang.
A hidden tang is always lower quality than a full tang.
Tang type describes construction; durability also depends on dimensions, materials, fit and intended loads.
Only forged knives can have a full tang.

question.explanation: The knowledge base explicitly rejects treating tang styles as a simple quality hierarchy.

recovery_questions.prompt: What makes a through tang different from a full tang?

options.text: A through tang is narrower and enclosed, but extends to and is secured at the butt.
A through tang has no steel inside the handle.
A full tang always stops before the butt.
There is no difference.

recovery_questions.explanation: A through tang is a hidden-tang construction that extends to the butt; it is not a full-outline tang.

recovery_questions.prompt: A welded bolster is visible in a production knife. What does that fact alone prove?

options.text: The knife is low quality.
The blade steel is cheap.
Nothing about overall quality without considering fit, joint quality, heat control and finishing.
The knife was not heat treated.

recovery_questions.explanation: A correctly executed separate bolster can be a rational manufacturing and structural choice.

content.lead: Most general-purpose kitchen knives sharpen from both sides, but 'double bevel' does not always mean perfectly symmetrical.
points: A symmetrical double bevel places comparable geometry on both sides.
An asymmetrical double bevel moves the edge closer to one side and can affect food release, precision and slight steering.
The exact grind matters more than assumptions based on the knife's name.
content.takeaway: Double bevel tells you there are two sharpened sides; it does not by itself tell you the exact symmetry.

question.prompt: What can an asymmetrical double bevel change?

options.text: Only the decorative finish.
Food separation and the tendency to steer slightly.
Whether the handle is full tang.
Whether the steel is stainless.

question.explanation: Moving the edge toward one side changes how the geometry interacts with food and can introduce slight steering.

recovery_questions.prompt: Does 'double bevel' guarantee a 50/50 symmetrical grind?

options.text: Yes, always.
No. Double bevel means both sides are sharpened; the proportions can be asymmetrical.
Only on forged knives.
Only on Japanese profiles.

recovery_questions.explanation: Symmetry is a separate property from the presence of two bevels.

recovery_questions.prompt: What should staff check before making a claim about the exact grind?

options.text: The silhouette alone.
The model's actual construction/specification.
The handle material.
The Damascus pattern.

recovery_questions.explanation: Profile names and appearances can be shared by knives with different grinds.

content.lead: Traditional single-bevel geometry can be handed and behaves differently from ordinary double-bevel sharpening.
points: Single-bevel knives concentrate the main bevel on one side and require a different sharpening approach.
Handedness and steering can matter, so the exact model must be checked before advising a customer.
A traditional profile name does not prove the grind: modern makers also produce double-bevel versions of traditionally single-bevel forms.
content.takeaway: Never infer handedness or sharpening instructions from the silhouette alone.

question.prompt: A knife has a profile traditionally associated with single-bevel construction. What should staff do?

options.text: Assume it is right-handed.
Assume it is single bevel and give traditional sharpening instructions.
Check the exact model's grind and handedness before describing or sharpening it.
Treat all versions as 50/50 double bevel.

question.explanation: The same profile name can exist in different grinds; model-specific verification is essential.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can single-bevel handedness matter to a customer?

options.text: It can affect steering, use and sharpening.
It changes the steel composition.
It determines whether the knife can cut vegetables.
It determines the handle material.

recovery_questions.explanation: The asymmetric working geometry can interact differently with the cut depending on orientation.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is unsafe product advice?

options.text: Checking the exact specification before explaining the grind.
Explaining that a profile name alone does not prove handedness.
Giving single-bevel sharpening instructions solely because the knife looks like a traditional single-bevel form.
Comparing verified model geometry.

recovery_questions.explanation: Sharpening advice must follow the actual grind, not a visual assumption.

questions.prompt: Which part is the rear of the cutting edge nearest the handle?

options.text: Heel
Spine
Tip
Pommel

questions.explanation: The heel is the rear of the cutting edge.

options.text: Full tang is always superior.
Construction type must be evaluated with dimensions, materials, fit and intended use.
A welded bolster proves low quality.
Hidden tang and through tang are identical terms.

questions.explanation: Construction features are not universal quality rankings.

questions.prompt: Can a double-bevel knife be asymmetrical?

options.text: Yes
No
Only if serrated
Only if forged

questions.explanation: Two bevels do not require a perfectly symmetrical ratio.

questions.prompt: What is the correct rule before describing handedness?

options.text: Infer it from the silhouette.
Infer it from the country of origin.
Check the exact model's grind and specification.
Assume every traditional profile is right-handed.

modules.title: Knife Shapes & Intended Use
modules.summary: Match blade families to the work they are designed to do instead of recommending by appearance alone.

lessons.title: Start from the work, not the silhouette

content.lead: The most useful sales question is not 'Which shape do you like?' but 'What do you actually cut?'
points: Ask what foods the customer cuts most often and in what quantities.
Ask whether the work is mainly on a board or in the hand, and whether it needs chopping, long slicing, work around bone, fish preparation or fine detail.
Use those answers to identify the blade family before comparing materials or appearance.

question.prompt: What should staff identify first when recommending a knife?

options.text: Preferred Damascus pattern
The customer's actual cutting work
Highest hardness available
Most expensive series

question.explanation: The source explicitly tells sales staff to start from the customer's work, not the silhouette they like.

recovery_questions.prompt: A customer says 'I want a bunka because I like the shape.' What is the best next question?

options.text: Which handle color?
What foods and cutting movements will you use it for most often?
Do you want the hardest steel?
Would you like a larger box?

recovery_questions.explanation: The intended work determines whether that shape is actually suitable.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which information is most useful before selecting a blade family?

options.text: Foods, quantities and cutting movements
Logo placement
Packaging size
Blade pattern only

recovery_questions.explanation: Those factors define the functional problem the knife must solve.

content.lead: Chef's knife, gyuto, santoku and Chinese cleaver can all be general-purpose tools, but they emphasize different movement and geometry.
points: Chef's knives and gyuto give useful length and versatility for broad kitchen work.
Santoku offers a compact all-round format with enough height for board work.
A Chinese cleaver can provide broad contact and food-transfer area, but its thin general-purpose versions are not automatically bone cleavers.
content.takeaway: General-purpose does not mean identical behavior.

question.prompt: Which statement about a Chinese cleaver is safest?

options.text: Every Chinese cleaver is designed for heavy bone
Thin general-purpose Chinese cleavers can be excellent board tools but should not be assumed to be bone cleavers
It is only for vegetables
It must be single bevel

question.explanation: Blade family names do not override the exact geometry and intended use.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why might a santoku appeal to someone who wants an all-round knife in a smaller format?

options.text: It combines compact length with useful blade height for board work
It is always heavier than a chef's knife
It is always single bevel
It is designed for bones

recovery_questions.explanation: Its compact general-purpose format is part of the reason the shape is widely useful.

recovery_questions.prompt: What should decide between two suitable general-purpose shapes?

options.text: Only which one looks more traditional
The customer's movements, preferred length and ergonomic fit
Only the higher HRC
Only the larger blade

recovery_questions.explanation: Once function is satisfied, movement and fit distinguish suitable options.

lessons.title: Use specialist geometry for specialist work

content.lead: Boning, filleting, carving and fish butchery ask for very different mechanical behavior.
points: A boning knife stays narrow so it can change angle around joints and bone.
A fillet knife may be flexible to follow fish contours; hard thin models should not be forced into deep bends or twisted.
A deba is a fish-butchery specialist: its strong heel can handle appropriate fish joints and small bones, but it is not a universal cleaver.
content.takeaway: Specialist shape describes a mechanical job, not a license for extra force.

question.prompt: Which use is appropriate for a deba?

options.text: Universal mammal-bone cleaving
Controlled fish-butchery work using different parts of the blade appropriately
Prying frozen food apart
Flexible filleting around a rib cage

question.explanation: The deba is specialized for fish butchery and must not be treated as a universal impact tool.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is a Western boning knife narrow?

options.text: To change angle easily while following joints and bone
To add chopping mass
To increase knuckle clearance
To act as a cleaver

recovery_questions.explanation: Low blade height helps the knife navigate a three-dimensional path around bone.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is wrong with testing how far a hard fillet knife can bend?

options.text: Nothing; maximum flex is the point
Excess lateral stress can chip, crack or fracture a hard thin blade
It removes the finish
It makes the handle heavier

recovery_questions.explanation: Use only the flex the model is designed to provide.

content.lead: Long narrow slicers are built to reduce repeated sawing and produce cleaner portions.
points: Carving and ham knives use length to create long drawing cuts through boneless cooked meat.
Traditional sashimi slicers use a long controlled pull cut through raw fish and can be single bevel and handed.
Length only helps if the user actually uses a long stroke rather than short repeated sawing.
content.takeaway: A slicer's advantage comes from using its length in the intended stroke.

question.prompt: What is the main reason for the length of a dedicated slicer?

options.text: To make the knife heavier for chopping
To complete broad portions with fewer, cleaner drawing strokes
To pry joints apart
To make the knife suitable for frozen food

question.explanation: Long slicing geometry reduces the need for repeated back-and-forth cuts.

recovery_questions.prompt: How should a traditional sashimi slicer normally be used?

options.text: With a long controlled pull stroke
As a rocking chopper
With sideways scraping
As a flexible fillet knife

recovery_questions.explanation: The geometry is optimized for clean draw slicing, not chopping or flexing.

recovery_questions.prompt: When does a long slicing blade provide little benefit?

options.text: When the user reduces every cut to short sawing strokes
When cutting boneless cooked meat
When making broad thin slices
When the food is stabilized

recovery_questions.explanation: The user has to exploit the available edge length.

questions.prompt: What comes first in a sound recommendation?

options.text: Customer's work
Pattern
Price ceiling only
Hardness only

questions.prompt: Can a thin Chinese cleaver be assumed to be a bone cleaver?

options.text: Yes
No
Only if stainless
Only if long

questions.explanation: Exact geometry and intended use must be checked.

questions.prompt: A fillet knife feels forced while bending around a contour. What should the user do?

options.text: Bend harder
Change the cutting angle instead of forcing more flex
Twist the blade
Strike the spine

questions.explanation: Do not exceed the flex the model is designed to provide.

questions.prompt: What makes a long slicer effective?

options.text: Using a long drawing stroke
Heavy vertical impact
Sideways leverage
Rapid rocking

questions.explanation: The blade length is useful when the stroke uses it.
